concepts.def: A recessive genetic disorder caused by a mutation in the CFTR gene, producing faulty chloride channels and thick, sticky mucus in the lungs and gut.
A membrane channel protein that transports chloride ions; a faulty version disrupts water movement and produces abnormally thick mucus.
A person with one normal and one faulty recessive allele who shows no symptoms but can pass the faulty allele to offspring.
A treatment that delivers a working copy of a gene, for example using a liposome or virus vector, into cells to correct a genetic disorder.
Testing DNA to detect alleles associated with genetic conditions, used in prenatal, carrier or pre-implantation contexts and raising ethical issues.
Movement of molecules or ions across a membrane against a concentration gradient, requiring carrier proteins and energy from ATP.

walkthroughs.body_html:
Genes & Health — a core area of A-Level Biology.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Genes & Health brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Genes & Health.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: Cystic fibrosis is inherited as a:
options: recessive allele
dominant allele
Y-linked allele
codominant allele

mcqs.q: The faulty CFTR protein causes symptoms because it cannot transport:
options: chloride ions across membranes
oxygen into the blood
glucose into cells
red blood cells to the lungs

mcqs.q: Two carrier parents (Ff x Ff) have a child. The probability the child is affected is:
options: 1 in 4
1 in 2
1 in 3
certain

mcqs.q: Gene therapy aims to treat cystic fibrosis by:
options: delivering a normal copy of the CFTR gene into cells
removing all chloride ions from the lungs
killing the bacteria that cause the mucus
replacing the patient's whole genome

mcqs.q: Why don't carriers of cystic fibrosis have symptoms?
options: Carriers have a mild form of cystic fibrosis.
The faulty protein causes the lungs to fill with extra blood.
Carriers are heterozygous; their one normal CFTR allele makes enough working protein, so the recessive faulty allele is masked.
Carriers cannot pass the faulty allele to their children.

mcqs.q: What does the faulty CFTR protein fail to do?
options: All children of two carriers will themselves be affected.
The faulty protein causes the lungs to fill with extra blood.
The faulty protein blocks oxygen from entering the lungs directly.
It cannot transport chloride ions across membranes, so water movement changes and mucus becomes thick and sticky.

mcqs.q: Two carriers have a child. What is the chance it is affected?
options: If the first child is affected, the next three will be healthy.
All children of two carriers will themselves be affected.
Each child has a 1 in 4 (25%) chance of being affected, independent of any previous children.
Carriers cannot pass the faulty allele to their children.
